doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Analog consoles and vintage microphones
summary: He recalls recording on four, eight, sixteen and twenty-four tracks and the cost of giant consoles and vintage microphones.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: guys. You’ve got to know the tech — and back then the technical part — like I was telling this class today here, the recording class, you know we recorded on this giant analog consoles, which are still the best. Well when I first started it was four track, then we went to George Massenburg and I went to Philadelphia to record at Sigma Sound because they had an eight track. But I started out on four track, then eight, then sixteen, then twenty-four, and then the digital stuff came in. But I was showing pictures today from the old days of those giant consoles which still are — in just a few studios today because they’re dinosaurs. And they’re so expensive. I was telling today, the mics in these studios, they’d have over a million dollars in microphones, just vintage microphones. And all the engineers that I’ve worked with — well it’s only been a few that I’ve worked with consistently, and they had their own racks of gear that would be wheeled into the studio in the control room. You know, equalization, compression, the mic preamps, the microphones. But most of the great studios, like Capitol in LA had millions of dollars — and still do — millions of dollars in vintage microphones. A single mic, like a classic Neumann or Telefunken or whatever, it could be fifteen grand there. A single microphone. So people trying to record now couldn’t afford a console that would stretch from the wall over to here and take three of us at the console. Nobody can afford that now.
